purpose: Anakinra is used to treat rheumatoid arthritis in adults when other medicines have not worked well enough. It is also used for certain rare inflammatory conditions, including a serious condition called Neonatal-Onset Multisystem Inflammatory Disease (NOMID) and other autoinflammatory syndromes. It helps reduce pain, swelling, and joint damage caused by inflammation.
how_it_works: Your body makes a natural protein called interleukin-1 (IL-1) that causes inflammation. In conditions like rheumatoid arthritis, your body makes too much of this protein, leading to painful swelling and joint damage. Anakinra works by blocking IL-1 from attaching to its target in your body, which helps calm down the overactive inflammation and relieve your symptoms.
common_side_effects: The most common side effect is redness, swelling, bruising, or pain at the injection site — this happens in many patients but usually gets better over time. You may also experience headache, nausea, or diarrhea. Some people get mild flu-like symptoms, especially when first starting the medication.
warnings: Anakinra can lower your ability to fight infections, so tell your doctor right away if you develop a fever, chills, or signs of infection. Do not use this medicine if you already have an active infection. You should not receive live vaccines while taking anakinra. People with kidney problems may need a dose adjustment, so make sure your doctor knows your full medical history. Rarely, serious allergic reactions can occur — seek emergency help if you have trouble breathing, rash, or swelling of the face.
typical_dosing: The usual dose for adults with rheumatoid arthritis is 100 mg injected just under the skin (subcutaneous injection) once every day. It is best to inject it at the same time each day. Your doctor or nurse will show you how to give yourself the injection at home. For children with certain autoinflammatory conditions, the dose is based on body weight and is determined by the doctor.
